title: Spans, Layers and Managers of Managers

know: How spans follow from team size and how layers follow from spans and headcount.
Larson's rules of thumb for managers and managers of managers, with their reasons.
What each layer costs: delay, distance from information, and salary.
believe: A layer is justified by the decisions only it can join; otherwise it is delay.
Managing managers is a different job from managing a team.
can_do: Compute the layers an organization of a given size needs and compare with what it has.
Recognize a span that is too wide or too narrow from its symptoms.
Say what a manager of managers should inspect and decide.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given an organization's size, team size and current layers, the reader says whether a layer is missing or surplus and what it costs.
acceptance_criteria.probe: An organization of 120 engineers has teams of seven, each with a manager, and all seventeen managers report to one VP. Using only this chapter: what is wrong, and what would you change?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A span of seventeen is far above what a manager of managers can sustain (Larson's rule of thumb is roughly four to six); add a layer of directors or group managers, at the cost of one more step for decisions, and say what that layer decides.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every number is presented as a named author's rule of thumb with its reason, and the chapter says what AI may change about it with labeled claims.
Each pattern in the chapter names its user and an outcome measure by which a reader could tell that it worked.

audience.who: Executives (CTO, CPO, VP, director) who draw or approve the reporting structure, and engineers and managers who live in it.
already_knows: Chapter 8's team sizes: Larson's six to eight engineers per manager, as a result with assumptions
What an engineering manager and a director are, loosely

thesis.question: Given the team sizes of chapter 8, how many people should a manager have, how many layers follow, and what does each layer cost?
thesis.claim: Given the team sizes of chapter 8, a manager should have as many people as they can know the work of and develop — for a line manager one team, for a manager of managers about four to six managers in Larson's rule of thumb — and the number of layers follows arithmetically from headcount and those spans; each layer adds a step of delay and distance from information, so a layer is kept only if it joins decisions across the units below it that those units cannot join themselves.
thesis.disputed_by: The delayering view that flatter is always better and managers are overhead, and the opposite habit of adding a layer to give senior people scope.
thesis.so_what: A leader derives the layer count before drawing the chart, states what each layer decides, and removes or merges a layer that only relays.
thesis.how_why: A manager's attention is finite: too many reports and they stop knowing the work, too few and they do the work themselves or meddle. Layers multiply spans, so the count follows from size; and since every layer delays decisions and filters information, it has to pay for itself in decisions joined.

supporting_claims.claim: A manager's span is limited by attention, the people whose work the manager can know and whom the manager can develop: for a line manager that is one team of chapter 8's size, for a manager of managers about four to six managers in Larson's rule of thumb, and a span outside the range shows in recognizable symptoms.
The number of layers follows arithmetically from headcount, team size and spans, so it can be computed before the chart is drawn and compared with the layers an organization has.

Each layer costs a step of delay, a step of distance from information and a small share of salary, so a layer is kept only if it joins decisions across the units below it that those units cannot join themselves, and a layer that only relays is removed or merged.

Managing managers is a different job from managing a team: the manager of managers no longer sees the work, so inspects it deliberately, decides what crosses teams, and leaves each team to its manager.

Neither the view that flatter is always better nor the habit of adding a layer to give a senior person scope survives the derivation: the answer is the fewest layers the spans allow, each with its decisions written down.

role.contribution: Derives the management structure between the top and the teams from the team sizes of Part II.

additional_patterns.applies_to: spans, layers, layer-cost: spans come before layers because layers are computed from them, and the count comes before its cost and purpose; the three patterns then apply the count, the purpose and the changed job of the person in the layer, in that order

flow.rationale: The reader first meets a span of twelve that nobody chose, and a later layer that slowed decisions, so both errors are on the table before any rule. Spans come next because layers are computed from them, and the cost and purpose of a layer after the count, because only then is there something to weigh. The three patterns apply spans and layers, purpose, and the changed job in that order. The disagreement between sources follows the patterns because its resolution, the fewest layers the spans allow, each with its decisions written, is the first two patterns taken together: placed before them it would be a slogan, placed after them it names what the reader has already seen done. The anti-patterns follow the resolution because they are the two disputed views in practice. The worked example comes after everything it uses, and AI last because it changes the inputs of a derivation the reader must already hold. Putting the Corvane arithmetic first would ask the reader to judge spans before knowing the ranges.

hook.content: In 2024 twelve engineering managers at Corvane reported to one VP Engineering, Dario Vance. Nobody had decided that the number should be twelve; in one month three requests for a new team reached him because there was nobody else to send them to. A year later Corvane put directors between him and the managers, and a year after that its engineers complained that decisions were slow.

bridge.from_reader_world: Most readers have worked under a manager with too many reports to know their work, or in a chart with a level nobody could explain, and have heard both that managers are overhead and that a growing company needs more of them.
bridge.to_topic: Both complaints are about numbers nobody derived: how many people a manager leads and how many levels follow. The previous chapter put a triad at every level; this one asks how many levels there are.

thesis_statement.text: A manager should have as many people as they can know the work of and develop: for a line manager one team, for a manager of managers about four to six managers in Larson's rule of thumb. The number of layers follows arithmetically from headcount and those spans, and since each layer adds a step of delay and distance from information, a layer is kept only if it joins decisions across the units below it that those units cannot join themselves.
thesis_statement.placement: KEY POINTS callout and the second lead paragraph (p02)

roadmap.placement: IN THIS CHAPTER callout and the second lead paragraph (p02)

promises.promise: See a span of twelve at Corvane that nobody chose, and the layer that later replaced it.
Learn what limits a span and what Larson's rules of thumb say for managers and managers of managers.
Compute the layers an organization needs from its headcount and spans.
Know what a layer costs and what it is for.
Use three patterns: derive the layers, write what each layer decides, and inspect as a manager of managers.
See where the sources disagree about adding and cutting layers, and the two usual ways layers go wrong.
Run the arithmetic on Corvane at four sizes, and see what AI may change.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In 2024 twelve engineering managers reported to Corvane's one VP Engineering, a number nobody had chosen, and the layer of directors that replaced it a year later brought a complaint of its own.

evidence.what: Corvane, 2024, 180 people: 95 engineers in eleven product teams and a platform team, each team with an engineering manager, all twelve reporting to Dario Vance, VP Engineering. Three requests for a new team reached him in one month. In 2025 directors were added; in 2026 engineers complained of slow decisions.
evidence.shows: Both a missing layer and the cost of a layer occur in one company within two years, and neither number was derived.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A span is limited by what a manager can know and develop, layers follow by arithmetic from headcount and spans, and a layer is kept only if it joins decisions the units below it cannot join themselves.

transition_in.carries_over: Two numbers nobody derived, and the previous chapter's triad that must exist at each level.
transition_in.introduces: How many levels there are and how many people each manager leads, as one claim, and the route through the chapter.

sections.heading: Setting the Scene: Twelve Managers and One VP
sections.controlling_idea: Corvane's span of twelve came from growth, not from a decision, and it cost attention to everything that lay between teams; the layer that replaced it cost delay.

advances_thesis.how: Shows a span too wide and a layer's cost in one company before any rule is given.

transition_in.carries_over: The span of twelve.
transition_in.introduces: How it arose and what it cost.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The span of twelve arose by growth: every new team got a manager, and nobody asked whom the managers would report to.

evidence.what: 2021, 50 people: about 24 engineers in four teams, two engineering managers with two teams each, reporting to Tomas Rell, the CTO. 2023: eleven product teams formed, each with an engineering manager, plus the platform team under Lena Brandt; Dario Vance joined as VP Engineering and all twelve managers reported to him.
evidence.shows: The number of managers was derived from the number of teams; the number of people those managers report to was not derived from anything.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md

paragraphs.controlling_idea: With twelve managers reporting to him the VP could answer what was brought to him and could not look at what lay between teams, and the directors added in 2025 brought a different cost, so the question is how many layers and what each is for.

evidence.what: 2024: the three requests for new teams in one month; the platform team's size not revisited while the engineers it served doubled; open launch requests grew every month for about a year before the 2024 change brief. 2026, about 500 people: quarterly planning took nine of thirteen weeks and the people deciding were two or three levels from the information.
evidence.shows: Too few layers and a layer both have a cost, so neither 'flatter' nor 'more managers' is the answer by itself.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md

transition_in.carries_over: Twelve managers under one VP.
transition_in.introduces: What that span cost, what the added layer cost, and the question.

sections.heading: Spans: How Many People One Manager Can Lead
sections.controlling_idea: A span is limited by the manager's attention; for a line manager it is one team, for a manager of managers Larson's four to six, and each end of each range has a symptom.

advances_thesis.how: Defines span and gives Larson's two rules of thumb with their reasons and the symptoms outside them.

flow.rationale: The definition and the limit come first, then the two kinds of manager in the order of the reporting line, then the symptoms, which need both ranges.

transition_in.carries_over: The question of how many layers and what each is for.
transition_in.introduces: The quantity layers are computed from: the span.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A span is the number of people who report directly to one manager, and what limits it is attention: a manager can lead as many people as they can know the work of and develop.

evidence.what: Definitions of span, line manager and manager of managers. Scope note: the chapter counts the engineering line, the largest; product managers and designers report in their own lines (chapter 18) and the same arithmetic applies to them.
evidence.shows: The limit is a property of the manager's time, not of the chart.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: For a line manager the span is one team, and chapter 8 already derived its size: six to eight engineers in Larson's rule of thumb, which this chapter takes as given.

evidence.what: Larson: a manager supports six to eight engineers; below four the manager becomes a tech lead manager, above eight or nine a coach and safety net. Chapter 8 derived the team size from scope, on-call and coordination, with a least of six that is the author's judgement. Larson: "Never leave managers supporting more than eight individuals."
evidence.shows: The first span is not a new number: it is the team size of chapter 8, so a line manager with two teams has left the range.
evidence.source: Will Larson, An Elegant Puzzle (2019); team-size-and-composition

transition_in.carries_over: A span limited by attention.
transition_in.introduces: The line manager's span, taken from chapter 8.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: For a manager of managers Larson's rule of thumb is four to six managers, with a reason at each end: below four the manager should still be learning the job or the domain, above six they can only solve problems as they arrive.

evidence.what: Larson: "Managers-of-managers should support four to six managers". Below four they should be in a period of active learning on the problem domain or on moving from supporting engineers to supporting managers. On the upper end: "supporting a large team of managers leaves you functioning purely as a problem-solving coach."
evidence.shows: The number is smaller than six to eight for a reason the author adds as his own reading: each report stands for a whole team, so knowing the work of five managers means knowing five teams' work at second hand.
evidence.source: Will Larson, An Elegant Puzzle (2019); author's notes

transition_in.carries_over: Six to eight engineers for a line manager.
transition_in.introduces: A smaller number for a manager whose reports are managers.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A span outside its range can be recognized from what the manager does all week and from what stops happening.

evidence.what: Table. Columns: Manager / Span / Larson's description / What you see (the author's reading). Rows: line manager below four (tech lead manager; writes much of the design and code, or meddles); line manager above eight or nine (coach and safety net; one-on-ones lapse, feedback and career talks stop first); manager of managers below four (ramping up; acceptable for a stated time, otherwise does the managers' jobs); manager of managers above six (problem-solving coach; hears only what is brought, nothing between teams gets looked at).
evidence.shows: The reader can diagnose a span from symptoms without the chart.
evidence.source: Will Larson, An Elegant Puzzle (2019); the author's record engineering-management-operating-model for the order in which things degrade

transition_in.carries_over: Two ranges, each with a reason at both ends.
transition_in.introduces: What it looks like when a span is outside its range.

sections.heading: Layers: The Arithmetic from Headcount to Levels
sections.controlling_idea: The number of layers is computed from headcount, team size and spans, and comparing the computed number with the real one shows a missing or a surplus layer.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the computation and the comparison the reader is asked to be able to do.

flow.rationale: The definition and the procedure first, then what it gives at each size, then the comparison with a real chart, which needs the table.

transition_in.carries_over: The two spans.
transition_in.introduces: The number of layers that follows from them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A layer is one level of managers in the reporting line, and the number of layers is found by dividing: engineers by team size, then managers by four to six, until six or fewer people are left to report to one leader.

evidence.what: Mermaid flowchart LR: "Engineers" -> "Teams: engineers divided by team size (chapter 8)" -> "Line managers: one per team" -> "More than six?"; yes -> "Add a layer: managers divided by four to six" -> back to the question; no -> "They report to one leader: stop and count the layers".
evidence.shows: Layers are an output of headcount and spans, not something chosen.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: With Larson's spans, one layer of managers carries up to about eight engineers, two up to about 48, three up to about 288 and four up to about 1,700, so a layer is added roughly every time the organization grows four- to sixfold.

evidence.what: Table. Columns: Layers of managers / Who is in them / Engineers, narrowest spans (teams of six, spans of four) / Engineers, widest spans (teams of eight, spans of six). Rows: 1: 6 / 8; 2: 24 / 48; 3: 96 / 288; 4: 384 / 1,728. The arithmetic is the author's, on Larson's numbers.
evidence.shows: The reader can read off the layers an organization of a given size needs.

evidence.what: Larson: "For every additional order of magnitude of engineers, you need to design and maintain a new layer of management."
evidence.shows: Larson states the same dependence more roughly; his own spans put the step at four- to sixfold growth, and the author reads the order of magnitude as the outer bound.
evidence.source: Will Larson, An Elegant Puzzle (2019); author's notes

transition_in.carries_over: The division.
transition_in.introduces: What it gives at each size.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Comparing the computed layers with the real ones gives two findings: a missing layer shows as a span above the range somewhere, a surplus layer as spans below four that nobody is growing into.

evidence.what: A generic case: 60 engineers in eight teams of seven or eight with eight managers reporting to one head: two layers where the table gives three, and a span of eight above the four to six. The reverse: 40 engineers in five teams with two directors and a VP: three layers where two would do, and spans of two and three.
evidence.shows: The comparison turns a feeling ('too many managers', 'my boss has no time') into a finding with a number.

transition_in.carries_over: The layers a size needs.
transition_in.introduces: The comparison with the layers an organization has.

sections.heading: What a Layer Costs, and What It Is For
sections.controlling_idea: A layer costs delay, distance from information and some salary, and it earns that cost only by joining decisions across the units below it that they cannot join themselves.

advances_thesis.how: States the three costs and the one justification, which is the test the patterns and anti-patterns use.

flow.rationale: The three costs run from the one that weighs most in the decision about a layer, delay, to the one that weighs least, salary; the purpose comes after them because it is what the costs are weighed against.

transition_in.carries_over: The arithmetic, which says how many layers the spans require.
transition_in.introduces: What each of those layers costs, which the arithmetic does not show.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The first cost is delay: every decision that has to pass through a layer waits there for one more person.

evidence.what: A question between two teams in different groups goes up to each manager, to each director, and to the person above both: with two layers two people are asked, with three layers four. Morieux and Tollman count 'waste and fewer mistakes that result from escalating decisions' among what removing layers saves.
evidence.shows: Delay grows with the number of layers a decision crosses, not with the number of managers.
evidence.source: Yves Morieux and Peter Tollman, Six Simple Rules (2014); author's notes

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The second cost is distance from information: each layer passes on a summary, so the person deciding at the top knows less than the people who asked.

evidence.what: Fournier, The Manager's Path, on managing managers: skip-level meetings exist partly to detect where you are being 'managed up' well to the detriment of the team; managers can make your life easier by hiding problems. The author's record managing-managers: every signal arrives pre-filtered, and a manager under pressure filters optimistically.
evidence.shows: Filtering needs no bad faith; it is what summarizing does, once per layer.
evidence.source: Camille Fournier, The Manager's Path (2017); managing-managers

evidence.what: Morieux and Tollman: decisions should be made as close as possible to where the action takes place and where information is richest.
evidence.shows: The same cost stated from the other side: a decision moved up moves away from its information.
evidence.source: Six Simple Rules (2014); author's notes

transition_in.carries_over: Delay.
transition_in.introduces: A second cost: what is lost at each step.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The third cost is salary, and it is the smallest: the first layer of managers is most of the management ratio, and each layer above adds about a fifth of the one below.

evidence.what: The author's arithmetic with teams of seven and spans of five: one manager per 7 engineers with one layer; 6 managers per 35 engineers with two (one per 5.8); 31 per 175 with three (one per 5.6). Larson makes 'set target ratio of management to individual contributors' a step of planning an organization change.
evidence.shows: Removing an upper layer saves little money, so the case for or against it rests on delay and distance.
evidence.source: Will Larson, An Elegant Puzzle (2019); author's notes

transition_in.carries_over: Two costs paid in time and knowledge.
transition_in.introduces: The cost paid in money, which is the least of the three.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A layer earns its cost by joining decisions across the units below it that those units cannot join themselves, and a layer with no such decisions only relays.

evidence.what: The test: list the decisions the layer made last quarter that involved more than one unit below it and that those units could not have settled between themselves (moving scope or people between teams, the order of work across teams, who manages each team). The idea of a leader joining decisions is Part V's; Morieux and Tollman's integrator, a role with both the interest and the power to make others cooperate, is the nearest concept in the sources.
evidence.shows: The same test justifies a layer and identifies one to remove.
evidence.source: journal-spec part-5 thesis; Six Simple Rules (2014)

transition_in.carries_over: Three costs every layer has.
transition_in.introduces: What a layer gives in return, and the test for it.

sections.heading: Pattern: Derive the Layers Before Drawing the Chart
sections.controlling_idea: The layer count is computed from projected headcount and spans before any names are placed, and a span outside its range is fixed with width before depth.

advances_thesis.how: Turns the arithmetic into steps a leader runs, with a user and an outcome measure.

transition_in.carries_over: The arithmetic and the test of a layer.
transition_in.introduces: The first of three patterns that use them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The pattern, for the leader who owns the reporting structure, is five steps from projected headcount to a layer count, measured by the number of managers whose span is outside its range.

evidence.what: User: the executive who owns the chart and the directors who propose changes to it. Outcome measure: the number of managers whose span is outside its range without a stated reason and end date, and whether the layers equal the computed number. Steps: project the headcount a year out; take team sizes from chapter 8; one line manager per team; divide by four to six until one leader remains; compare with the chart and write a reason and a date for every span outside the range. The first and third of Larson's steps for planning an organization change are 'project head count a year out' and 'set target ratio of management to individual contributors'. Step 4 is the division of the layers section (Figure 1), cited and not repeated; the pattern adds the projected headcount, the comparison and the measure.
evidence.shows: The count is fixed before the question of who gets which box is raised.
evidence.source: Will Larson, An Elegant Puzzle (2019); author's notes

paragraphs.controlling_idea: When a span comes out above its range, add a peer before adding a layer: width costs one more manager, depth costs every decision a step.

evidence.what: Eight managers under one director become two groups of four under two directors without a new layer if the level above has room; a new layer is needed only when the top span itself is over the range. This is the author's recommendation; it does not hold when the level above is already at six.
evidence.shows: The arithmetic leaves a choice at the edges of the ranges, and the costs of a layer say which way to take it.

transition_in.carries_over: The comparison in the last step.
transition_in.introduces: What to do when a span is too wide.

sections.heading: Pattern: Write What Each Layer Decides
sections.controlling_idea: Each layer gets a short written list of the decisions it makes and the ones it leaves below, and a layer for which the list is empty is merged.

advances_thesis.how: Makes the purpose test a document, with a user and an outcome measure.

transition_in.carries_over: A layer count that the spans justify.
transition_in.introduces: The second pattern: saying what each of those layers decides.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The pattern, for each manager of managers and the leader above, is one page per layer of what it decides and what it leaves to the layer below, found by looking back at where last quarter's decisions between teams were settled, and measured by where such decisions are settled and how long they take.

evidence.what: User: every manager of managers and the leader they report to. Outcome measure: the share of decisions between teams settled at the lowest layer that spans the teams involved, and the median days from question to decision. Table. Columns: Layer / Decides / Leaves to the layer below. Rows: line manager (who works on what in the team, hiring and growth of each person, with the product manager the team's quarter / how the work is done); manager of managers (moving scope and people between its teams, the order of work across them within the outcomes given, who manages each team, disputes between two of its teams / anything inside one team); head of engineering (the same between groups, standards and shared areas, how many engineers each group gets / anything inside one group). The rows are the author's; chapter 18's page of decisions is the same instrument at the top. The page is found by looking back: collect last quarter's decisions between teams and note the layer at which each was settled; a layer at which none was settled is a candidate for merging. Allocating decision rights in general is chapter 22's.
evidence.shows: A layer's purpose is checkable when it is a list of decisions.
evidence.source: executive-roles-and-reporting-lines; the author's judgement

sections.heading: Pattern: Inspect What You No Longer See
sections.controlling_idea: A manager of managers has a different job from a line manager: the work is out of sight, so they inspect it on purpose, decide what crosses teams and hold each manager accountable for the team.

advances_thesis.how: Says what changes when the reports are managers, and what a manager of managers inspects and decides.

transition_in.carries_over: A layer that decides only what crosses teams.
transition_in.introduces: The third pattern: how the person in that layer knows enough to decide.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Managing managers is a different job because the manager no longer sees the work: what a line manager learns by being in the team, a manager of managers learns only by asking.

evidence.what: Fournier: "People who are good at managing a single team, or even a couple of related teams, fall apart when asked to manage managers, or teams that are outside of their skill set."
evidence.shows: The step is a change of job, not more of the same.
evidence.source: Camille Fournier, The Manager's Path (2017); author's notes

evidence.what: Zhuo, The Making of a Manager: as the team grows it matters less how good the manager is at the work and more how much of a multiplier effect she has. Grove's High Output Management is on the author's bookshelf without notes; its description there says it is about maximizing an organization's output through delegation, clear communication and focused management, and nothing more is taken from it.
evidence.shows: Two more sources place the manager's output in other people's work.
evidence.source: Julie Zhuo, The Making of a Manager (2019); author's bookshelf

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The pattern, for a manager of managers, is a fixed set of things to look at every week and quarter, measured by how many problems reach them by escalation, resignation or incident before their own inspection found them.

evidence.what: User: a manager of managers. Outcome measure: problems that reached them by escalation, resignation or incident before inspection (the revisiting test of the author's record managing-managers). List: each team's flow and health measures (release frequency, incident load, lead time); whether each team can state its goals and why (Fournier's first question when debugging a team); hiring, goals and postmortems followed up 'until you figure out what you don't need to follow up on' (Fournier); skip-level meetings, 'perhaps once a quarter' (Fournier); each manager's one-on-ones and feedback, closely for a new manager. Skip-level meeting defined. Inspection as support, from the author's record inspected-trust.
evidence.shows: Inspection replaces what being in the team used to supply.
evidence.source: Camille Fournier, The Manager's Path (2017); managing-managers; managing-multiple-teams; inspected-trust

transition_in.carries_over: Work that is out of sight.
transition_in.introduces: What to look at, for whom, and how to tell it works.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: What a manager of managers decides is what crosses teams, and what they must not do is take a team's problem back from its manager.

evidence.what: Fournier's three cases (unstable roadmap, errant tech lead, firefighting) end with the same answer: the manager is accountable for the health and productivity of the team. The author's record: accountability that is absorbed upward stops being accountability; a manager who passes requests down and status up without judgement is a relay.
evidence.shows: The layer joins and inspects; it does not manage the teams a second time.
evidence.source: Camille Fournier, The Manager's Path (2017); managing-managers

transition_in.carries_over: What is inspected.
transition_in.introduces: What is decided, and what is left with the manager.

sections.heading: Where the Sources Disagree: Add a Layer or Cut One
sections.controlling_idea: Larson adds layers as an organization grows and Morieux and Tollman cut them first; both object to a layer that joins nothing, and the resolution is the fewest layers the spans allow.

advances_thesis.how: Answers the delayering view with the sources, and states the book's resolution.

transition_in.carries_over: Three patterns that all assume layers are needed.
transition_in.introduces: A source that says to cut them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Larson designs a new layer as the organization grows and keeps spans narrow enough to invest in people, while Morieux and Tollman make cutting layers the first step, widening spans on purpose.

evidence.what: Morieux and Tollman: "the first step in reinforcing your managers to play the integrator role is to cut the number of hierarchical layers, which simultaneously increases the span of control and shortens hierarchical lines." They also advise removing managerial positions that will never have enough power to influence the work. Integrator defined. This is the source behind the delayering view that flatter is always better.
evidence.shows: The two sources give opposite first moves: one adds a layer at a size, the other removes one.
evidence.source: Six Simple Rules (2014); An Elegant Puzzle (2019); author's notes

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The two agree on the test, a layer must have decisions that make others cooperate, and differ in where they start, so the resolution is the fewest layers that keep spans inside Larson's ranges, each with its decisions written down, which is what the first two patterns already do.

evidence.what: The author's reading: Morieux and Tollman write against layers that cannot add value; Larson writes for growing engineering organizations that have too few. Neither says flatter is always better. Table. Columns: Choice / What you gain / What you give up / Right when. Rows: wide and flat (spans above the range, fewer layers: short lines, decisions near the work / managers who only coach, nothing between teams looked at / experienced managers, stable teams, little that crosses teams); narrow and deep (spans below the range, more layers: time for each person / a step of delay and filtering per layer, managers who do their reports' jobs / briefly, while a manager grows into a span); in range (the fewest layers that keep spans within four to six / some of each cost / the default).
evidence.shows: The disagreement becomes a choice with conditions, and 'flatter is always better' is the wide row taken as a rule.
evidence.source: Six Simple Rules (2014); An Elegant Puzzle (2019); the author's judgement

transition_in.carries_over: Two opposite first moves.
transition_in.introduces: What the two share, and the book's resolution.

sections.heading: Anti-Patterns: The Relay Layer and the Layer Made for a Person
sections.controlling_idea: Layers go wrong in two usual ways: a layer that passes things on without deciding, and a layer created to give someone scope.

advances_thesis.how: Names the two failures the purpose test catches, with the book's failure-pattern names.

transition_in.carries_over: The test that a layer must have decisions of its own.
transition_in.introduces: Two layers that fail it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The relay layer passes requests down and status up and decides nothing, which makes it one more rung of the Escalation Ladder.

evidence.what: The failure pattern The Escalation Ladder: decisions travel upward to someone with less information. The author's record managing-managers names the relay manager. Sign: questions between two teams of the same group are settled above the group.
evidence.shows: A relay layer has all three costs and none of the return.
evidence.source: where-product-and-tech-organizations-go-wrong; managing-managers

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The layer made for a person exists to give a senior manager scope or a title, and it can be recognized by removing the name and asking which decisions the role joins.

evidence.what: Fournier on empire builders, who seek to grow their teams and mandates without concern for what is best for the organization. Chapter 18's test for a role made to fit a person: remove the name and ask which decisions the role joins. When the chart is redrawn for this reason it is also The Reorg as Strategy. Signs: spans of two or three with no end date; a layer added in the same month as a retention conversation.
evidence.shows: The second disputed habit of the thesis, adding a layer to give senior people scope, fails the same test as the relay.
evidence.source: Camille Fournier, The Manager's Path (2017); executive-roles-and-reporting-lines

transition_in.carries_over: A layer that decides nothing.
transition_in.introduces: A layer that was never meant to decide anything.

sections.heading: Worked Example: Corvane's Layers at Four Sizes
sections.controlling_idea: Run at four sizes, the arithmetic shows Corvane one layer short in 2024, at the right count with wide spans and unwritten decisions in 2026, and due a fourth layer by 2028.

advances_thesis.how: Applies the computation and the purpose test to ledger numbers.

flow.rationale: The table first, then the stages in the order they happened, so that each reading uses the stage before it; the 2028 projection stays in the table.

transition_in.carries_over: The arithmetic, the test and the patterns.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The table sets, for Corvane in 2021, 2024 and 2026 and as a projection for 2028, the layers the arithmetic gives beside the layers and spans the company had.

evidence.what: Table. Columns: Year and size / Teams and line managers / Layers the arithmetic gives / What Corvane had / Widest span. Rows: 2021, 50 people, about 24 engineers: four teams; two layers; two layers (two engineering managers, the CTO); about twelve engineers per manager. 2024, 180 people, 95 engineers: twelve teams, twelve managers; three layers (two or three managers of managers); two layers; twelve managers under the VP. 2026, 500 people, 260 in product and tech: about thirty product teams and the platform team; three layers (five to eight directors); three layers (four group directors, the Director of Platform, the VP); seven or eight managers per group director; the VP has six. 2028, 1,100 people, 520 in product and tech: about sixty teams if the proportion of 2026 holds; four layers (ten to fifteen directors, two or three leaders above them); not stated beyond two business units. Layers are counted up to the person who runs engineering, Dario Vance; Tomas Rell as CTO holds technical direction above him (chapter 18).
evidence.shows: The computed and the actual number can be set side by side for each stage.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In 2021 the layer count was right and the spans were double the range, and in 2024 a whole layer was missing, which is the span of twelve the chapter opened with.

evidence.what: 2021: each manager had two teams and about twelve engineers, Larson's coach and safety net. 2024: twelve managers need two or three managers of managers; Corvane had none, so every decision between two teams went to Dario Vance or was not made: the three requests for new teams, the platform team's size.
evidence.shows: The symptoms of the scene are the ones the span table predicts.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md

transition_in.introduces: What they show.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In 2026 Corvane had the three layers the arithmetic gives, with directors' spans above the range, and the cost its engineers felt came from a layer whose decisions had not been written.

evidence.what: Mermaid flowchart TB: "Dario Vance, VP Engineering" -> four nodes "Engineering director, product group N: 7 or 8 managers", -> "Lena Brandt, Director of Platform", -> "Security lead"; one director -> "Engineering managers, one per team" -> "Teams of six to eight engineers".
evidence.shows: Three layers, the top span within the range and the directors' spans above it.

evidence.what: 2026, about 500 people: the Nine-Week Plan, agreed across the four groups with every director; the Tuesday Reorg drawn up by people who did not know what each team ran; three senior engineers leaving one group citing slow decisions. Late in 2026 Dario Vance and the directors wrote one page of what a director decides without him (moving scope and people between the group's teams, the order of work within the group's outcomes, who manages each team) and what goes to him (anything that touches two groups or a shared area). No result is recorded. The author's reading: remove nothing; the remedy for spans of seven or eight is a fifth and sixth group when the product allows, not a fourth layer.
evidence.shows: A layer of the right count still costs delay when what it decides is unwritten.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md

sections.heading: What AI Changes Here
sections.controlling_idea: AI may change the inputs of the derivation, team size and the cost of gathering information, and as of November 2026 there is no measurement showing that it widens the span a manager can sustain.

advances_thesis.how: Says which inputs of the derivation AI may move, with labeled claims, and leaves the full argument to chapter 36.

transition_in.carries_over: A derivation with inputs: team size and spans.
transition_in.introduces: What AI may do to those inputs.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: AI already takes over part of a manager's information gathering, and that does not widen the span, because the limit was never the gathering.

evidence.what: Label scheme announced. Emerging (the author's observation, as of November 2026): managers use AI tools to summarize status, pull requests and incident reports. The span is limited by knowing the work well enough to judge it and by developing each person, which are conversations. No Proven claim: the author knows of no published measurement of sustainable span with AI.
evidence.shows: A cheaper summary changes the cost of one part of the job and not its limit.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: What AI does to layers depends on what it does to team size, and both directions are possible.

evidence.what: Speculative. If teams settle nearer chapter 8's floors, at four or five engineers, the same headcount means more teams and more line managers, or managers leading two small teams; if teams keep their size and own more, the arithmetic is unchanged. A second speculative claim: an engineer who directs several coding agents is doing a kind of supervision, and whether that counts against the manager's span is open. What would confirm: organizations reporting stable spans above the ranges with unchanged attrition and promotion rates. Full argument in team-shape-and-roles-with-ai.
evidence.shows: The derivation stays; its inputs may move, and it is run again when they do.
evidence.source: team-size-and-composition; team-shape-and-roles-with-ai

transition_in.carries_over: A span that AI does not widen by itself.
transition_in.introduces: The layer count, which may move through team size.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: Spans and layers are one calculation with two prices. The spans come from what one person can know and develop, the layers from dividing headcount by the spans, and the count this gives is a minimum the organization needs and a maximum it should tolerate: one layer fewer and somebody has twelve reports and looks at nothing between teams, one layer more and every decision waits a step for someone who knows less.
conclusion.so_what: The reader can compute the layers an organization needs, say whether one is missing or surplus and what it costs, recognize a span that is too wide or too narrow from its symptoms, and say what a manager of managers inspects and decides.

callback.to: The twelve engineering managers who reported to Dario Vance in 2024, and the directors whose layer slowed decisions in 2026.
callback.how: The reader can now say that twelve was a missing layer by Larson's four to six, and that the layer added in 2025 was the right count with its decisions unwritten.

takeaway.content: Compute the layers your organization needs from its headcount and spans, compare with the chart, and for each layer write the decisions it makes that the layer below cannot. The checklist gives the steps.
